652.title: Yom Kippur: ask first
652.hook: before the day, people ask one another's forgiveness
652.howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, especially on its eve, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness (mechilah), and many say a prayer before Kol Nidre declaring that they forgive anyone who wronged them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat Shuvah and Hosea's call. Your line was return. Which dropped good thing did you go back to? Today, the one thing Yom Kippur can't do by itself. Day six hundred fifty-two.

The afternoon before Yom Kippur has its own sounds. Phones buzzing with messages: if I hurt you this year, I'm sorry. Neighbors stopping each other on the street. A teenager, mortified, knocking on a sister's bedroom door. Some of it is a little formal, a habit. Some of it is the hardest conversation of the year. People do this because of one line in the Mishnah, and once you hear it, the whole holiday looks different.
screen: `PHONES BUZZING: I'M SORRY.` → `A KNOCK ON A SISTER'S DOOR.` → `ONE LINE IN THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: The line is at the very end of tractate Yoma, the Mishnah's book about Yom Kippur. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone, until you have appeased the other person. Read that again. The holiest day of the year, a whole day of fasting and prayer, the high point of the calendar, cannot fix what you did to your neighbor. Only your neighbor can. So you go first. You ask. The Talmud and later law work out the details with real psychological sense. You should be specific, not vague. If the person refuses, you try again, up to three times, and bring a few friends along to help make peace. If they still refuse after that, the burden lifts from you. And there's a rule for the other side, too. Maimonides writes that a person shouldn't be cruel and refuse to forgive. When someone sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart and a willing spirit. Not every hurt can be fixed in an afternoon. Teachers are careful to say that forgiveness isn't the same as trust, and that no one is required to put themselves back in danger. But the shape is clear. Before you stand before God asking to be forgiven, stand in front of the people you hurt. Then the day can do its work. The word for this kind of forgiveness, mechilah, has the sense of letting go of a debt.
screen: `BETWEEN YOU AND GOD.` · `BETWEEN YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `UP TO THREE TIMES.` · `DON'T BE CRUEL; FORGIVE.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask forgiveness from someone. Bring to mind one person you hurt, even a little: a sharp word, a broken promise, a silence. Picture their face. Find the specific thing. Now say, quietly, the words you'd use: I'm sorry for, and the thing itself. Then decide how you'll reach them, today or soon. If you pray, you can ask God for the courage to make the call. Then, for a moment, think of someone who might be waiting to ask you. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, which, the Mishnah says, can't atone for wrongs between people until they make peace.
Your line: ask before the day. Today, make the call or send the message: I'm sorry for, and the specific thing. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: Yom Kippur: releasing vows
653.hook: the evening begins by annulling rash vows, sung three times
653.howItsDone: Kol Nidre is chanted at the start of Yom Kippur evening, before sunset, with Torah scrolls held beside the cantor; it is repeated three times and followed by the verse from Numbers 15:26.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's rule: wrongs between people need the people first. Your line was ask before the day. Did you make the call? Today, the first words of Yom Kippur itself. Day six hundred fifty-three.

The sun is still up. The synagogue is fuller than at any other time of year. Many are dressed in white. The ark opens, and Torah scrolls are carried out and held, one on each side of the prayer leader, like witnesses. The room goes quiet. And then the cantor begins a melody so famous that composers have written concert pieces on it. The words aren't a prayer at all. They're a legal formula, in Aramaic. And they're sung three times, each time a little louder.
screen: `THE FULLEST NIGHT OF THE YEAR.` → `SCROLLS HELD LIKE WITNESSES.` → `A LEGAL FORMULA, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Kol Nidre means all vows. The text declares that all vows, oaths and promises we make to God, and fail to keep, are released, void, not binding. Why open the holiest day with that? The Torah takes vows seriously: "When a man voweth a vow unto the LORD, or sweareth an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word." People in every generation make rash promises to God in a moment of fear or anger: if I get through this, I'll never, I'll always. And then they can't keep them. Kol Nidre is a way of clearing those words before standing in judgment. Before it begins, a line is said giving permission to pray together with sinners, with everyone, whatever their past. Then, right after, comes a verse from Numbers: the whole community shall be forgiven, "and the stranger that sojourneth among them." Some important limits. Kol Nidre covers only personal vows between a person and God. It has never released promises made to other people, contracts or oaths in court. Medieval rabbis argued about it, and some great authorities wanted it removed. In later centuries, enemies of the Jews twisted it into a false charge that a Jew's word couldn't be trusted, which it never meant. Rabbeinu Tam, in the twelfth century, changed the wording to look forward: vows from this Yom Kippur to the next. Many Ashkenazi communities say it that way. Its staying power may be the melody, and the honesty. Everyone in the room knows they've said things to heaven they didn't keep.
screen: `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `RASH PROMISES TO GOD.` · `NEVER PROMISES TO PEOPLE.` · `FROM THIS YOM KIPPUR TO THE NEXT.` · then, large: `RELEASE THE VOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one rash promise. Think of something you vowed to yourself, or to heaven, in a hard moment, that you haven't kept and maybe never could. I'll never eat sugar again. I'll call every day. Name it honestly. Then let it go, not with guilt, but with relief. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask to be released. If not, simply say: I set this down. Then think about whether a smaller, real promise belongs in its place. The bell holds the time.
Kol Nidre. All vows. The Aramaic formula, sung three times at the start of Yom Kippur, releasing unkept personal vows to God.
Your line: release the vows. Today, before you make a big promise to yourself, make it small enough to keep. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Yom Kippur: white
654.hook: many wear white, like angels and like burial shrouds
654.tomorrow: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day
654.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi communities men wear a white kittel on Yom Kippur (and some on Rosh Hashanah); women and Sephardi worshippers often dress in white; many avoid leather shoes on Yom Kippur as one of the day's afflictions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kol Nidre, all vows, sung three times before sunset. Your line was release the vows. Did you set one rash promise down? Today, what people are wearing in that room. Day six hundred fifty-four.

Look around a traditional synagogue on Yom Kippur night and the colors are gone. Men in plain white robes over their clothes, tied with a simple belt. Women in white blouses and dresses. White covers on the ark and the reading table. Feet in canvas sneakers or socks, because many don't wear leather today. It looks a little like a wedding, and a little like a funeral. In a way, it's both.
screen: `THE COLORS ARE GONE.` → `PLAIN WHITE ROBES.` → `A WEDDING, AND A FUNERAL.`

segments.voice: The white robe is called a kittel, a Yiddish word for a smock. It's simple: white cotton or linen, no pockets to speak of, often tied with a white belt. In many Ashkenazi communities, men wear it on Yom Kippur, and some on Rosh Hashanah too. And it shows up at the big doors of a life. Many grooms wear a kittel under the wedding canopy. Many leaders of the Passover seder wear one. And many are buried in one, or in plain white shrouds like it. Why white on Yom Kippur? The great sixteenth-century authority Rabbi Moshe Isserles gives two reasons, and they pull in opposite directions. First, white is the clothing of angels. On this day, without food or drink, people are said to be like angels, beyond the body's needs, praising all day long. Second, the kittel is like a burial shroud. Wearing it humbles the heart: it reminds you that life is short and that you'll stand before God with nothing but who you've been. Both meanings at once: pure and mortal, angelic and dust. And behind both is a verse from Isaiah, quoted all through these days: "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." Sephardi communities don't usually wear the kittel itself, but many dress in white. And white clothing isn't a rule for everyone; it's a widespread custom. The point isn't fashion. When everyone wears the same plain white, the rich and the poor look alike. You stand there as a person, nothing more.
screen: `KITTEL: A WHITE SMOCK.` · `WEDDING, SEDER, BURIAL.` · `LIKE ANGELS.` · `LIKE A SHROUD.` · then, large: `DRESSED IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something plain. If you can, change into something simple: a plain shirt, no logos, no jewelry, nothing that says who you are to the world. If you can't change, take off one thing, a watch or a ring. Then sit. Notice what's left when the signals are gone. If you pray, you can picture standing before God dressed like everyone else. If not, picture standing in a room where nobody can tell who's important. The bell holds the time.
Kittel. The plain white robe worn on Yom Kippur, at weddings and at the seder, like an angel's garment and like a shroud.
Your line: dressed in white. Today, treat one person as if you could no longer see any of the signs of status on them. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day
655.hook: the service retells the high priest entering the holy of holies
655.howItsDone: During the Musaf service of Yom Kippur, the prayer leader chants the Avodah, a poetic account of the high priest's service, and in many Ashkenazi congregations worshippers kneel and bow fully to the floor when the high priest's confession is recalled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kittel, white like angels and like shrouds. Your line was dressed in white. Could you see someone without their status? Today, another man in white, two thousand years ago. Day six hundred fifty-five.

Late on Yom Kippur morning, something unusual happens in many synagogues. The prayer leader begins to tell a story. Not pray it. Tell it, step by step, like a narrator. And at certain lines, the whole congregation does something they do on no other day: they get down on their knees and bow their foreheads to the floor. The story they're telling is about one man, in one room, on one day of the year, in a Temple that has not stood for nearly two thousand years.
screen: `THE LEADER TELLS A STORY.` → `FOREHEADS TO THE FLOOR.` → `ONE MAN, ONE ROOM, ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: This is the Avodah, the service: a poetic retelling of the high priest's work on Yom Kippur, based on Leviticus sixteen and the Mishnah's tractate Yoma. The Torah's rule was strict. The high priest could enter the innermost room of the sanctuary, the holy of holies, only on this day, once in the year. The day was long and exacting. He changed his clothes five times, immersed his body each time, and wore simple white linen for the holiest parts. He confessed three times: for himself and his household, for the priests, for all Israel. And in those confessions he spoke God's four-letter name aloud, the name no one else ever pronounced. The Mishnah says that when the people in the courtyard heard it, they knelt, bowed, fell on their faces, and called out: blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. That's the moment congregations reenact on the floor today. Then he went in alone, carrying burning coals and incense, into a small dark room. And here's a detail the Mishnah preserves. Coming out, he said only a short prayer in the outer room. He didn't linger, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside. Everyone was holding their breath. The Torah gives the purpose: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." The Mishnah adds that he made a feast for his friends when he came out safely. Today, with no Temple, words take the place of the service. Once a year, the whole room tells the story.
screen: `AVODAH: THE SERVICE.` · `WHITE LINEN, FIVE CHANGES.` · `THE NAME, AND FACES ON THE FLOOR.` · `A SHORT PRAYER COMING OUT.` · then, large: `ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture one holy moment. Think of a moment in your life that felt set apart: a birth, a death, a vow, a silence under a huge sky. Something that happened once and couldn't be repeated. Go back to it. Where were you standing? What did the air feel like? Who was waiting outside? If you pray, you can thank God for it. If not, just let it be holy again for a minute, without explaining it. The bell holds the time.
Avodah. Service. The Yom Kippur retelling of the high priest's day, when congregations bow to the floor at the sound of the Name.
Your line: once a year. Today, name one thing you do only once a year, and decide to do it with full attention when it comes. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: Yom Kippur: Jonah
656.hook: the afternoon reads Jonah, and the whole city of Nineveh turns
656.howItsDone: At the afternoon (Mincha) service of Yom Kippur, the entire book of Jonah is chanted as the haftarah, followed by verses from Micah in many communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Avodah, the high priest's day. Your line was once a year. What's your once-a-year thing? Today, the late afternoon of Yom Kippur, when people are hungry and tired, and someone reads a story about a fish. Day six hundred fifty-six.

It's three or four in the afternoon. The fast is nearly a day old. Heads ache. Somebody's dozing in the back row. And now, at the afternoon service, the reader chants the whole book of Jonah. Four short chapters. A prophet runs away from God, gets thrown off a ship in a storm, spends three days inside a great fish, and finally goes where he was sent. Most people remember the fish. The rabbis chose this story for this hour because of what happens after the fish.
screen: `THREE IN THE AFTERNOON, FASTING.` → `A PROPHET RUNS.` → `AFTER THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Jonah is sent to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, the empire that terrorized his people. That's why he runs. He doesn't want them to have a chance. When he finally arrives, he preaches what may be the shortest sermon in the Bible: five Hebrew words, yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. And then, astonishingly, it works. The people of Nineveh believe. They fast. Everyone puts on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king gets up from his throne, sits in ashes, and orders even the animals to fast. And then the line: "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, which He said He would do unto them; and He did it not." The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, points out exactly what that verse says and doesn't say. It doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says God saw their works. Their deeds changed. That's a sharp message for a room full of people who are fasting right now. The fast is not the point. What you do afterward is. The book ends with Jonah angry, sitting outside the city, and God asking him a question about mercy: should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, "and also much cattle?" The book ends on that question. It doesn't tell us Jonah's answer. If even Nineveh can turn, the reasoning goes, so can anyone in this room.
screen: `NINEVEH, THE ENEMY CITY.` · `FIVE WORDS, AND THEY TURN.` · `NOT THE SACKCLOTH: THEIR WORKS.` · `A BOOK THAT ENDS ON A QUESTION.` · then, large: `EVEN NINEVEH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: believe someone can change. Think of a person you've written off. Not someone dangerous: someone you've decided is just like that and always will be. A relative, an old friend, a coworker. Hold their face in your mind. Now imagine them, a year from now, having changed one thing. Let yourself picture it. If you pray, you can pray for their turning, and for your own patience. If not, simply leave the door open a crack. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, whose afternoon reading is Jonah, and a whole enemy city that turned.
Your line: even Nineveh. Today, notice one small change in someone you'd given up on, and tell them you noticed. Day six hundred fifty-six.

657.title: Yom Kippur: one long blast
657.hook: Neilah ends with a single long shofar note and "next year in Jerusalem"
657.howItsDone: The Neilah service closes Yom Kippur with the ark open throughout; it ends with the Shema, 'Baruch shem' three times, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, a single long shofar blast and 'next year in Jerusalem.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah and the city that turned. Your line was even Nineveh. Did you notice a change in someone you'd given up on? Today, the last hour of Yom Kippur. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

The sun is going down. It's been about twenty-five hours without food or water. People who've been sitting all day stand up, because the ark has been opened, and it will stay open for the entire last service. Nobody wants to sit while the ark is open. Legs ache. Voices are hoarse. And yet many people say this final hour is the one they wait for all year. The service has a name that sounds like a door swinging shut.
screen: `THE SUN GOING DOWN.` → `THE ARK STAYS OPEN.` → `A DOOR SWINGING SHUT.`

segments.voice: It's called Neilah, the closing, or the locking. The ancient sources debate what's being closed. One view: the gates of the Temple, locked at the end of the day. Another: the gates of heaven, closing as the day ends. Either way, the image is a gate, and it's still open, just barely. The words change. All through the ten days, the prayers asked: write us in the book of life. Now, in Neilah, they ask: seal us. Chotmenu. This is the last chance to get the wording right. The service builds. And then, at the very end, comes a sequence everyone knows. The congregation says the Shema's first line once. Then blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom, three times, out loud, the line usually whispered. Then a verse from Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, when the people saw fire fall from heaven and cried out: "The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God." It's said seven times, louder each time. And then the shofar. Not the long sets of Rosh Hashanah. One single, long blast, a tekiah gedolah, held as long as the blower's breath will last. And everyone answers together: l'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim. Next year in Jerusalem. It's an odd way to end. Not we did it, or we're forgiven. It ends with hope pointed forward. A long sound that doesn't break, and a promise about next year. Then people go home and eat.
screen: `NEILAH: THE CLOSING OF THE GATES.` · `WRITE US BECOMES SEAL US.` · `ONCE, THREE TIMES, SEVEN TIMES.` · `NEXT YEAR IN JERUSALEM.` · then, large: `ONE LONG BLAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end something with hope. Think of something that's ending soon: a day, a week, a project, a season, even a hard chapter. Picture its last moment. Now find a forward-pointing line to end it with: next time, or next year, or I'll be back. Breathe in, and then let out one long breath, the longest you can, like the last shofar note. If you pray, let that breath carry a hope to God. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, which ends at Neilah with one long blast of the shofar and next year in Jerusalem.
Your line: one long blast. Today, end your day with one long breath out, and one sentence of hope for tomorrow. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: From fasting to building
658.hook: many hammer the first nail of the sukkah as Yom Kippur ends
658.howItsDone: Many Jews begin building their sukkah on the night Yom Kippur ends, even if only by hammering one nail or setting up one pole, then finish it in the days before Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neilah, the closing gate. Your line was one long blast. Did your day end with a long breath and a hope? Today, what happens about ten minutes after that blast. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Yom Kippur is over. Stars are out. People pour out of the synagogue, dizzy with hunger, heading for bagels and orange juice. And in some backyards, before anyone has even sat down to eat, there's a strange sound. Tap, tap, tap. Someone is out in the dark with a hammer and a flashlight, banging in a single nail, or setting up one pole. Then they go inside and eat. They've started building a hut.
screen: `STARS OUT, FAST OVER.` → `TAP, TAP, TAP.` → `ONE NAIL, THEN DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hut is a sukkah, the temporary booth for the festival of Sukkot, which begins just five days after Yom Kippur. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." Rabbi Moshe Isserles, the great Ashkenazi authority, records the custom: right after Yom Kippur, begin building the sukkah, so as to go from one mitzvah to the next. Some just hammer one nail that night, a token. Others put up the whole frame. The idea behind it is old. A psalm says of the faithful: "They go from strength to strength." The rabbis read that as a rule of life. Don't leave a gap after something holy. When you finish one good thing, start the next while the energy is still warm. And look at the contrast. For ten days the focus was inward: judgment, books, confession, a day without food. Now the very next act is outward and physical: wood, nails, branches, a roof you can see the stars through. The year doesn't stay in the synagogue. The calendar itself moves the mood from awe to joy, from fasting to building. Some teachers add a gentle reason.
